phases.note: Math you can picture, ML you can code
LLM and agent design, mocks weekly

skills.label: Python + NumPy fluency
skills.what: Comfortable, fast Python with NumPy arrays, broadcasting, and vectorized code. Jupyter as a lab notebook.
skills.why: You write Python for automation already. The gap is thinking in tensors instead of loops, which every later week assumes.

skills.label: Linear algebra
skills.what: Vectors, matrices, dot products, matrix multiply as transformation, eigen-intuition. Not proofs, pictures.
skills.why: A transformer is matrix multiplies. If a weight matrix is not a picture in your head, nanoGPT will be noise.

skills.label: Calculus + chain rule
skills.what: Derivatives as sensitivity, partial derivatives, the chain rule. That is 90% of what deep learning uses.
skills.why: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied by a program. micrograd will make no sense without it.

skills.label: Probability + stats
skills.what: Distributions, expectation, softmax as a distribution, cross-entropy and log-likelihood.
skills.why: Every loss you will ever plot is a log-probability. Sampling from a model is sampling from a distribution.

skills.label: ML basics + gradient descent
skills.what: Linear and logistic regression, loss functions, gradient descent, overfitting, train/val/test splits.
skills.why: This is the smallest complete version of what a frontier lab does: a model, a loss, an optimizer, an eval.

skills.label: PyTorch
skills.what: Tensors, autograd, nn.Module, DataLoader, training loop, saving and loading, GPU device handling.
skills.why: The lingua franca of every lab. Your CUDA and cluster work later is PyTorch underneath.

skills.label: AI engineering (RAG, agents, evals)
skills.what: A twelve-rung ladder, from zero: the API call, structured outputs and tools, embeddings, basic RAG, measuring retrieval, advanced RAG, MCP, workflows with approval gates, agents with state, agent control, agent evals, and a CI loop. Each rung is a short course to watch and a small thing to build without a framework.
skills.why: What product-AI companies hire for, and the practical half of agentic system design later. Each rung assumes only the ones below it. If you can do a rung's build in under 20 minutes from blank, tick it and move on.

skills.label: Neural nets + backprop
skills.what: Build a neural network and its backward pass by hand (micrograd), then an MLP with batchnorm, then debug activations and gradients.
skills.why: This is the moment you stop treating models as black boxes. Everything after is scale and structure.

skills.label: Language modeling (makemore)
skills.what: Character-level language models: bigram, MLP, WaveNet-style. Loss curves, learning-rate sweeps, initialization.
skills.why: The first time you train a model that generates text. Also the first time you debug a training run, which is a research skill.

skills.label: Transformers (nanoGPT)
skills.what: Attention from scratch, multi-head, positional information, residuals and layer norm, the GPT block. nanoGPT line by line.
skills.why: The architecture every target company builds on. You must be able to write it blind.

skills.label: Tokenization
skills.what: Byte-pair encoding, why tokenizers cause so many model quirks, implementing minbpe.
skills.why: Tokenization sits between infra and modeling; it is a common source of production bugs and a common interview topic.

skills.label: Your first real training run
skills.what: Reproduce GPT-2 (124M) training on rented GPUs: mixed precision, torch.compile, data loading, logging, checkpoints, HellaSwag eval.
skills.why: Your first end-to-end run is the credential that says you have trained a model, not just called one. It also connects directly to your fleet experience.

skills.label: LLM stack + papers
skills.what: Read the canonical papers: the transformer, GPT-2/3, scaling laws, Llama 3, InstructGPT, DPO. Then Stanford CS336 lectures.
skills.why: Research engineers read papers weekly. This is the habit and the shared vocabulary you need to talk to researchers.

skills.label: Post-training + fine-tuning
skills.what: Supervised fine-tuning, LoRA, preference optimization with TRL, evaluating whether a fine-tune actually helped.
skills.why: Post-training is where most applied research happens today and it is cheap to do yourself.

skills.label: GPU programming
skills.what: How a GPU executes work, memory hierarchy, why bandwidth dominates, profiling, Triton kernels, FlashAttention's idea.
skills.why: Performance engineering is a top hiring lane at Anthropic and OpenAI, and your systems instincts transfer directly.

skills.label: Distributed training
skills.what: Data, tensor, pipeline parallelism; FSDP; NCCL; checkpointing; straggler and failure handling at scale.
skills.why: This is your home turf at a deeper level. Fleet reliability for a 10,000-GPU run is a live research problem in every lab.

skills.label: Inference + serving
skills.what: KV cache, paged attention, continuous batching, speculative decoding, quantization, serving on Kubernetes with vLLM and llm-d.
skills.why: Inference infrastructure is a common way into labs. It sits directly on top of the platform layer: scheduling, networking, and observability.

skills.label: Evaluation + alignment literacy
skills.what: Benchmarks and their failure modes, lm-eval-harness, Inspect, agentic evals, RLHF and Constitutional AI, first steps in interpretability.
skills.why: Evaluation infrastructure is a research engineering specialty and a natural extension of your observability background.

skills.label: Research project
skills.what: A ten-week project with a hypothesis, baseline, ablation, and writeup, in the training-reliability, inference, or agent-evaluation space.
skills.why: The single artifact that turns a systems engineer into a research engineer candidate.

skills.label: Public work + community
skills.what: Monthly writeups, merged open-source PRs, active presence in two communities, a mentor log.
skills.why: This is how mentors and referrals happen for someone without a lab or a university.

skills.label: Data structures + algorithms
skills.what: Hard-first: graphs (BFS/DFS, topological sort, union-find, shortest paths, MST, bridges), trees and tries, four weeks of dynamic programming, heaps, backtracking, monotonic stack, binary search on the answer. Then the easier patterns as a sweep. 169 problems in the DSA bank, with three timed problems a week for the rest of the plan.
skills.why: Coding rounds at every target company assume this. The bank is the road; Design Gurus is the map; Striver and Fiset are the deep sources for DP and graphs.

skills.label: Design principles + patterns
skills.what: SOLID and the design principles behind it, the patterns that show up in real systems, concurrency primitives, and the practical coding problems labs like: LRU cache, rate limiter, job scheduler.
skills.why: Practical coding rounds and the 'design this class' questions. Also makes your scaffolding reviews sharper.

skills.label: Distributed system design
skills.what: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Raft and the MIT distributed systems lectures, and the classic design interviews: feeds, queues, key-value stores, chat, schedulers, monitoring, storage.
skills.why: The biggest part of your loops, and where your platform experience turns into stories. Monitoring and scheduler designs are ones you have actually built.

skills.label: Data-heavy systems
skills.what: Streaming and batch, Kafka and Flink concepts, lakehouse formats, exactly-once, real-time analytics, recommendation and fraud pipelines.
skills.why: Data-heavy design rounds and the data side of ML platforms. An OTA is full of these systems, so you have real examples.

skills.label: ML platform design
skills.what: Designing ML Systems: features, training pipelines, serving, monitoring; designing a serving platform and a training cluster for a large run.
skills.why: The design round for ML infrastructure roles at the labs. Months 7 and 8 of the AI track are the hands-on version.

skills.label: LLM + agentic system design
skills.what: RAG at scale, LLM gateways with routing and cost control, eval pipelines, agent orchestration with sandboxing, memory, approvals, and observability.
skills.why: The newest interview topic and the one closest to what you already build. Anthropic's own engineering posts are the source material.

skills.label: Interview loops
skills.what: Full mock loops: timed coding, design, ML fundamentals, behavioral stories from your own record of past projects, and a research talk. Two mocks a week in the final months.
skills.why: Practice under time pressure is the only thing that converts knowledge into offers.

skills.label: Applications + offers
skills.what: Portfolio, resume rewrite for research-engineering roles, targeted applications, referrals from the rooms, offers and negotiation.
skills.why: The plan ends with real applications to the companies you named, backed by twelve artifacts, a research writeup, and interview fluency.

dsa_bank.topic: Graphs: BFS and DFS on grids and adjacency lists
dsa_bank.note: Write BFS and DFS templates from memory first: iterative and recursive, on a grid and on an adjacency list. Then the problems.
Kahn's algorithm and DFS post-order, both from memory. Know how to detect a cycle with each.

problems.name: Find All Possible Recipes from Given Supplies
Largest Color Value in a Directed Graph
Sort Items by Groups Respecting Dependencies

dsa_bank.note: Path compression and union by rank from memory. Know when union-find beats DFS: dynamic connectivity and Kruskal.

problems.name: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
Min Cost to Connect All Points

dsa_bank.topic: Advanced graphs: shortest paths, MST, bridges, Eulerian paths
dsa_bank.note: Dijkstra with a heap, Bellman-Ford, Prim, Kruskal, Tarjan's bridges, Hierholzer. Fiset's playlist is the source; write each once from memory before the problems.

problems.name: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in MST

dsa_bank.topic: Trees: DFS returns, path problems, BST properties
dsa_bank.note: Every tree problem is 'what does the recursive call return, and what does the parent do with it'. Write that sentence before coding each one.

problems.name: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
Kth Smallest Element in a BST
Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder
Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree

dsa_bank.topic: Trees II: views and orders, tries, segment trees and BIT
dsa_bank.note: Implement a trie, a segment tree with point update and range query, and a Fenwick tree from memory. Then the problems.

problems.name: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
Amount of Time for Binary Tree to Be Infected
Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

dsa_bank.note: For each: write the recursion with memo first, then tabulate, then space-optimize. Striver's series does exactly this order; follow it.

dsa_bank.topic: Dynamic programming II: 2-D grids and two-string DP
dsa_bank.note: Draw the table for every problem before coding. The bug is always the boundary row or column.

problems.name: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix

dsa_bank.topic: Dynamic programming III: knapsack, palindromes, stock and game DP
dsa_bank.note: Knapsack is the Design Gurus strength; read its chapter, then do these. State the choice at each index out loud.

problems.name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV

dsa_bank.topic: Dynamic programming IV: intervals, bitmask, state machines
dsa_bank.pattern: DP on intervals and subsets (beyond the course)
dsa_bank.note: These are the hard-round problems. Two a day is a good week; it is fine if several take a second attempt.

problems.name: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick
Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets

dsa_bank.topic: Heaps: two heaps, top-K, K-way merge
dsa_bank.pattern: Two Heaps; Top K Elements; K-way Merge
dsa_bank.note: Design Gurus' three heap chapters are its best material after knapsack. Implement a heap from scratch once, then never again.

problems.name: Kth Largest Element in an Array
Kth Largest Element in a Stream
Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers

dsa_bank.topic: Backtracking, monotonic stack, binary search on the answer
dsa_bank.pattern: Backtracking; Monotonic Stack; Modified Binary Search
dsa_bank.note: Three patterns that look unrelated and all come down to 'what is the invariant'. Write it above each solution.

problems.name: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days

dsa_bank.note: Each in 45 minutes from a blank file with tests. These are closer to lab coding rounds than any puzzle: state, invariants, and clean interfaces under time.

dsa_bank.topic: Pattern sweep I: sliding window and two pointers
dsa_bank.note: The easier Design Gurus patterns, done fast for maintenance. Your grokking repo already has two of these folders.

dsa_bank.topic: Pattern sweep II: fast and slow pointers, in-place reversal, cyclic sort
dsa_bank.pattern: Fast & Slow Pointers; In-place Reversal of a LinkedList; Cyclic Sort
dsa_bank.note: Linked-list and index-as-value tricks. Fast, mechanical, worth one week.

problems.name: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
